🎓 Main Feature

The 10x PMM Curriculum: What's Coming

Every PMM team now has access to AI tools. But access isn't leverage. Most PMMs are still using AI like a faster search engine — "write me a blog post," "summarize this call." The output is fine. Generic. Forgettable.

The gap isn't tools. It's behavior. That's why we built a structured 12-week curriculum designed to close the gap between having AI and actually using it to multiply your impact.

The Frame: Co-Work, Don't Outsource

Outsourcing (wrong): "Write this for me."
First draft shipped. Skill atrophies. Output is generic.

Co-working (right): "Push back on my thinking."
Iterate like sparring partners. Skill compounds. Output is distinctive.

💡 The 10x PMM isn't doing 10x the output.

It's the one whose judgment is 10x harder to replicate. AI handles drafts, research, rewrites. You reinvest that time in customer conversations, narrative, and original POV.

Three Phases, 12 Weeks

Weeks 1-2

Foundations

Prompting, tool stack, governance

Weeks 3-5

Co-Working

Drafting, research, real deliverables

Weeks 6-12

Building

Interactive artifacts, agent workflows

The Weekly Rhythm

Content alone doesn't change behavior. Rhythm does:

Monday
15-min module drop
Wednesday
30-min office hours
Friday
2-min demo share

Learning + Doing + Sharing. The Friday demo is the forcing function — when you know you'll show your work publicly, you actually do the work. Portfolio compounds.

Cohort starts May 12. Graduation August 10. By Sapphire 2026, every PMM will have a portfolio of AI-assisted work — not a certificate of attendance.

📖 Deep Dive

The Third Commercial Transformation

The enterprise software industry is in the middle of its third major commercial transformation in twenty-five years. The first moved software from perpetual licenses to subscription. The second introduced consumption pricing, led by AWS, Snowflake, and Databricks. The third — the arrival of agentic software — is the most difficult because the commercial unit is genuinely unclear for the first time in the history of the industry.

The Three Eras

  • Perpetual License (1990s–2000s): Named user, annual maintenance. Oracle, SAP, Siebel.
  • Subscription/SaaS (2000s–Present): Seat per month, tiered by edition. Salesforce, Workday, ServiceNow.
  • Consumption (2010s–Present): Usage — compute, API calls, data scanned. AWS, Snowflake, Stripe.
  • Agentic/Outcome (2024–): Conversation, resolution, or unlimited access to agentic capacity. Salesforce AELA, Microsoft Copilot, Intercom Fin.

Why It's Hard

A seat doesn't make sense when no human touches the product at the moment of value creation. Consumption makes partial sense, but agents use model calls, tool calls, and orchestration in proportions that vary wildly. Outcome-based pricing is theoretically correct — but the instrumentation to price on outcome doesn't yet exist in most enterprise relationships.

"Three vendors, three different commercial answers to the same underlying problem, within a single twelve-month window. That is not a stable market. It is a market in active redefinition."

The PMM Implication

The narrative and the commercial motion have to be architected together. A category leader cannot indefinitely sell a story whose central claim lives behind an upsell. If the agentic narrative is the future, but conversational capabilities are packaged as premium tier upgrades, customers notice when the narrative and the contract stop rhyming.

The vendors that invest early in closing the gap between story and contract are the ones that extend their lead. For PMMs, that means operating adjacent to product management and pricing in ways most marketing organizations aren't currently structured for.

The AI Adoption Gap

5%
of marketing leaders not piloting AI agents
report significant gains on business outcomes

Meanwhile, 70% of enterprise marketers are already implementing or planning to implement GenAI within six months. And 65% of CMOs say AI will dramatically change their role in the next two years.

The gap is clear: those who aren't piloting agents aren't seeing gains. The question isn't whether to adopt — it's how fast you can close the gap between access and leverage.
